utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Appearances. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone. Mark Harmon, Bronagh McKenna, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. Mr. Perisic is represented today by Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, Daniela Tasic, Colleen Rohan, and our interns are here, Katharine Marshall and Jason Keck, and Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith and Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Lukic. We go through the ritual, still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we begin, Mr. Lukic, I guess because Mr. Starcevic is not able to talk to anybody, he has sent word to the Chamber to say that he would like to leave tomorrow if it is at all possible, and I don't know -- it's not in my hands. It's not in the Chamber's hands. It's in the hands of counsel. Do you think can you give him that guarantee?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned he most certainly can because I'm going to complete my cross in half an hour today. But I don't know if this is all that significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You wouldn't need the whole two session and the whole day tomorrow too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I think we can reassure Mr. Starcevic that can he go home tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Starcevic, see I'm a good lawyer, Mr. Starcevic. You'll get my bill. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I got no translation, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just asked to go into private session, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session. 25 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Starcevic, if you recall yesterday, we finished with a number of documents that referred to the procedure that had to do with that person, Vujic, about whom there was a disciplinary court of the VRS disciplinary court, and then we established that he had been pensioned off by the Army of Yugoslavia. And you agreed with me that it indicated that he - let me put this that way - was terminated from active military service on different grounds which was stated in the decision of the disciplinary court. Now we're going to look at a document that you also looked at with Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at document P2417, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you said for this document that you established that this was also a sentence or a judgement by the disciplinary court of the VRS, and there was a legal remedy involved also, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then you also analysed for Mr. Harmon the sequence of events as far as proceedings for Antic, Zoran. We also see the entire judgement here pertaining to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up a little bit, please, so that we can see the particulars. This part is excellent and can we please look at the same section in the English. Probably it's on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What it says here in the particulars as we say that in the legal world, under number 2, about Antic, Zoran, at the time the judgement was reached and that was on the 23rd of September, 1995, and in parentheses, and it cannot be seen on the screen right now. This is something, probably, that we can see, and it does say that in the document. That, according to the particulars, he is currently at an unknown address in the VRS from the 15th of March 1995 [as interpreted] -- from the 15th of February, 1995 [as interpreted]. And then we have the dispositive or the main body of the sentence where it states --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpretation said 1995. I read.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 15th of February, 1993. We apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Madam Interpreter -- or Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, no -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it says, "Are guilty." Meaning specifically what it says at the end of this first paragraph. The second accused or co-accused Antic, Zoran, on 13th of March, 1995. Is that actually the date when he actually left the unit of his own will -- wilfully?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Simply speaking that is the day of his desertion? I'm using some easier language; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up, or, actually, scroll down this B/C/S part of. The English version of the text does not need to be moved. Can we scroll down a little bit more, please, so that we can see the heading of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please confirm for me that this judgement was reached on the 23rd of September, 1995. That is the day when the court practically established his guilt; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Compared to the previous case, Mr. Harmon did not show you a single document which would indicate that that man appeared as a serviceman in the Army of Yugoslavia. You didn't see any document indicating that that man, after this point in time, when he deserted, was in any unit of the Army of Yugoslavia or the Army of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on the assumption that this Mr. Antic, as well as based on the assumption in the first case of Mr. Kosojevic, when he left that unit of the Republika Srpska that he never went to any other unit of the Army of Yugoslavia. Would you agree with me that the person who has the duty to establish, in administrative terms, the day that all the rights due cease --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in order for rights to be suspended or cease for somebody, there has to be established a ground for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry -- apologise to the interpreter. I'm going to have to repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because my whole question was not recorded in the transcript, and I don't want to paraphrase, I'm going to answer -- I'm going to repeat. You would agree with me that if a certain person does not return to a unit of the Army of Yugoslavia and left the unit of the Army of Republika Srpska as established in this judgement, then the Republika Srpska has to establish, in the administrative sense, that his status has ended -- the status based on which he achieves or exercises his statutory rights.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In order for these rights to be terminated, a certain basis or certain grounds are required.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at document 1D03-0129 on the screen, please. We still need to remain in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this document carefully, Mr. Starcevic. I'm going to ask you about the contents, but I'm going to ask you about the form. This is what Mr. Harmon also asked you about. From this document, we can first see that it is dated the -- July 18th, 1995. I'm going to call it, and you're going to tell me if you agree with that term that it is a letter or missive of the chief of the General Staff of the VJ sent to the chief of the Main Staff of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in its a form this is a letter. We could also say that it is a recommendation, also, as well as a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to put the next question about. Based on these contents and the way Mr. Perisic is addressing Mr. Mrksic, we can see that from the words "kindly," and so on and so forth "influence," can it be seen from this kind of address that there was any kind of hierarchical relationship between Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Perisic and these two armies?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document does not indicate any form of hierarchy, because in a hierarchy, you would not kindly ask somebody but you would issue an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. I propose that this document be tendered into evidence, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see the relationship between this document and this witness. Under the guidelines, I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you throwing in the towel?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I'm going to propose that the document be tendered as a MFI, and then when we finish the examination of Mr. Starcevic, I'm going to talk about my earlier remarks in terms of Mr. Harmon, and I'm going to discuss my proposal. I will probably propose that all of this be withdrawn, but, any way, to follow the rules, I would now like to tender this document and propose it for -- that it be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, my objection stand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Even for marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It can be marked for identification [Microphone not activated] defer the argument on this until a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would need to -- then I would still need to state my position, if you agree. Mr. Harmon asked Mr. Starcevic about that document which was a warning or contained a warning, if you recall that. And he and he talked about the form of that document, so in the same -- along the same lines, I propose that this document too be tendered and marked for identification, until we state our arguments on that whole matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's try to save time. Mr. Harmon said you will argue this later. You will argue later, okay? It's admitted and marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number. Do you want it under seal or not under seal? Under seal, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D125, marked for identification, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document that I would like to show Mr. Starcevic is also under seal, and I would like us to then still remain in private session. This is 1D03-0128.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this document, Mr. Starcevic, and then after you look at it -- or when you need it to be scold up, just let us know. Mr. Starcevic, this document, signed by the chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and in its introduction, it refers to security, and it also refers to BG, BG means [B/C/S spoken] readiness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's an order sent to the 1st Army Command of the air force and the anti-aircraft defence. KS, do you remember what that is? Do you recall what that is?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. I think it could be one of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps if I were to tell you that these were special units, do you perhaps know this abbreviation SBK, what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that refers to the area of Slavonia and Baranja, and it's the Slavonia Baranja Corps. And the SOB is actual territory of Slavonia and Baranja, [B/C/S spoken] Slavonia Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This Slavonia Baranja Corps was not part of the Yugoslav Army; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by this order, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you ask the witness about KS. Where is KS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see KSJ next to the title which says order sent to the command of the 1st Army RV and PVO and then KSJ. That means special units corps of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: KSJ I see. I didn't see KS. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what I said and what was not recorded on page 9, line 17, my question about the SBO or, rather, SBK, that stands for Slavonia Baranja Corps. And the witness gave an answer. Now, in your answer, you said that it wasn't judging by this order. Now let me ask you this: This document, even in visual terms, is significantly -- makes a very clear distinction between two terms, "I order," and the other is "I recommend" or "I command" and "I recommend"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, in this portion which means -- which says that Mr. Perisic gives an order, Item 1 reads as follows: "Keep all current measures of combat readiness of the territory of the FRY." Now this is a classic example of an order issued by the chief of the General Staff to his units deployed in the territory for which is he responsible under the law.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you just say this area is outside FRY? If it is outside -- if it is outside the FRY, is it under his -- is it under his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my next question, because, with regard to this territory, he didn't issue an order -- let me ask the witness about this. I'm not going make any suggestions in this respect, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, in this part in which Mr. Perisic is recommending -- his recommendation refers to the territory of Slavonia and Baranja district, which is the territory outside the FRY, over which, under the Law on the Army, he has no jurisdiction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this recommendation can clearly be construed as a mode of cooperation between two armies that have similar strategic positions.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether it was cooperation or not, but in any case, this is not a binding document, which indicates that there was a desire to offer assistance in resolving the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for this document to be marked for MFI, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection to that status, Your Honour. I have no objection to that status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The document is admitted into evidence, marked for identification, and kept under seal. May it please be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D126, marked for identification, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at one more document? Or, actually, two, but while we're in private session; that's P2018. This is also under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we've seen -- we saw similar documents, but I chose to show you this one again, because Mr. Harmon asked you about this letter. This is a letter issued by the Army of Republika Srpska, judging by what you see in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was issued on the 8th of March, 2002. This is a decision taken after the president of the Republic had issued a decree relating to the persons for which he has jurisdiction, and in light of the rank of Mr. Mladic, this was under the jurisdiction of the president of the Republic. Would you agree with me that according to this decision until the 28th February 2002 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down, slow down, slow down. Carry on. 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- that Mr. Ratko Mladic, until that date, enjoyed the status of an officer of the Army of Republika Srpska, according to this document, and was serving there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, we can go back to an open session. This is going to be my last question, and, as I promised, with this, I will conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Harmon [sic] -- I beg your pardon, you -- sorry. Sorry, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one more question, and for that purpose, I would need document P2024 to be shown on the screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document is not chronologically in sequence with the previous document, but I wanted to show it to you in an open session. Can you please look at this document, sir. You will agree with me, Mr. Starcevic, that this is another document from the president of Republika Srpska as the commander in chief of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is mention here of the term that you also explained, which means a placing an individual at the disposal, which means that this particular person is still in the army but does not have a particular post as per establishment.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one can say that. He is still in professional service but is not discharging duties in any of the posts envisaged by the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to this document, judging by the date, Mr. Ratko Mladic was still in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to this document, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have hereby concluded my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we just return to Prosecution Exhibit 2024 that was on the screen a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Starcevic, the date of this document is 8.11.1996 and the effect of this document is that General Mladic is put at the disposal of the VRS General Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This document relies on the authority of Article 369 of the Law on the Army of the Republika Srpska. Do you know the contents of that law, by chance? Do you happen to recall what that is? This is the Law on the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can presume that this is an article of the law which governs the methodology of placing someone at the disposal and the duration of that. But I would really prefer to look at the law. I don't want to talk about legal regulations offhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you will bear with me for a minute, I have the law in front of me, and I just want to consult what that provision is, and maybe I can assist you. This is my question, Mr. Starcevic. Under the VJ law, when someone is put at the disposal of the army, is there a finite period of time on which they could remain at the disposal of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is, definitely a specified period, and if I remember correctly, that period could not last longer than two years. Again, if my memory serves me well, that could stretch over a period of five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me -- let me come back to that in a minute because I will have my colleague find the right provision. It's my recollection, Mr. Starcevic, that somebody could be put at the disposal in the VJ for a period not to exceed six months. I will find the text, I will re-educate myself, and I'll show it to you to give you the advantage of consulting with that text before you answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was precisely the reason why I said that I am not in favour of quoting something out of memory, because memory is not a good ally in such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just give me a minute, if I could, Your Honour, to consult with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, take a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will find that provision in just a moment, Mr. Starcevic, on the Law on the Army, and I will be back to you in a couple of minutes with a question about this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon wanted to ask a question relating to the Law on The Yugoslav Army and the one -- the article that governs this particular matter is 63 in the Law on the Yugoslav Army. I think this is what Mr. Harmon had in mind when he put this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, but this one is not Yugoslav law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand. I want to start my question, first of all, with the Yugoslav law. And if we could have P197 on the monitor for the benefit of Mr. Starcevic and for the Court's benefit. If we ... if you can go to Article 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, again, get me ask you a question. Is there a period of time during which a person in the VJ can remain on standby, or on -- at the disposal of the army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is an finite period and another proof that memory cannot always be relied upon. You were right when you said that this period was six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute you're running ahead of me. Where is the six months, and does standby mean putting at the disposal of the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the bottom of the English, Article 63, there is the term set forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, can you answer the Judge's question, whether standby, the term standby is the same as being placed at the disposal?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It seems this is how it was translated, this term from our legislature which is at the disposal, they translated it with the term standby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 2 of that article, would a person who is, for any reason, unfit to perform his duty be at the disposal of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They would be placed at the disposal, if they're unfit to perform the current duty, and there is no possibility for this person to find him a suitable post corresponding to their qualifications and capabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we go back to the previous exhibit -- I'm sorry, let me just get the right exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but ... yes, thank you very much. It's P2024. Perhaps counsel can assist me. Could I have -- I'm looking for the exhibit number for the Law on the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have P191 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the basis of putting General Mladic at the disposal was Article 369.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we go to 369 of this ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you enlarge it, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Starcevic, under which subpart of Article 369 of the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska was there authority to place General Mladic at the disposal of the army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Item 3 of this Article 369.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be more precise, paragraph 1, Item 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, under the Law on the Army of the Republika Srpska, was there an equivalent provision, as far as you know, as to how long a period of time an officer, under Article 369, could you placed at the disposal of the army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose there was such a provision, because placing someone at the disposal is, in a way, in an unnatural order of things. If you wanted to grant some legal security for members of the military, you have to put a certain time-limit. And I suppose that this provision should be sought in this law under the chapter that regulates the status-related issues of military servicemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 2018, which you saw earlier, Mr. Starcevic, was -- is that in private session, 2018?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we go into private session then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And could we have 2018 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 2018, which is the decision of, I believe, it was Mrs. Plavsic, as I recall, relieving General Mladic of his professional military service -- let me just wait to see the English text. Is dated the 8th of March, 2002, about six years after he had been placed on the disposal of the VRS. Can you reconcile for us, Mr. Starcevic, the disparity between him being placed on the disposal in 1996, his being relieved six years later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Scroll the English down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot specifically say, because I don't see the provision of the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska limiting the length of time one can spend being at the disposal. I assume it's similar to the provision in the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, but I'm just assuming that. In order to be sure, I would have to see whether there is an limit on the period. One can do that just like in the Army of Yugoslavia. If yes, then this is it a violation of the law to the detriment or prejudicial to Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we go back to the -- P191, please, which is the Law on the Army of the Republika Srpska, the VRS. And could we go to Article 163, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you scroll the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you scroll down, or up in the English? We need to see the entirety of Article 163. Thank you. Unfortunately, we have the English version on two separate pages, but we're on -- the text of the remaining part of 163 appears in the upper left-hand corner of the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, can you tell me in the Army of the Republika Srpska if there's a limit on how long someone can be placed -- a soldier can be placed at the disposal of the army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is an deadline, and, again, that is six months in this law, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, again, can you reconcile, then, the disparity of General Mladic remaining at the disposal of the VRS for six years? How do you reconcile that in light of the statutory text that's before you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This cannot be reconciled. This is it an evident violation of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't want to interfere that much, but, in view of this deadline, or term of six month, the witness was not told whether he had returned to some duty or not. It is the assumption of Mr. Harmon at some point, maybe, but only on that basis, perhaps, can one give an answer to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't know if that is an objection or -- a speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know either --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, know. What I mean is that the way that Mr. Harmon put the question, whether his question was intended to have him available from the point of it -- that he did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I don't understand what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're asked to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the law, this period that somebody is at the disposal somewhere else can be six month. If Mr. Harmon is putting this question, he needs to put the assumption, whether from the point in time the decision was made he was at the disposal for these six years, and that he, then, never, in that time, returned to any other establishment post. Perhaps we can seek an answer to that question, otherwise we're in the sphere of speculation. The position of Mr. -- if that is the position of Mr. Harmon, and that is the witness's answer, then I don't have any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you have an objection to that then you must adduce evidence to show that that period was interrupted. And unless you can do that, what do we then do?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if that is the position of Mr. Harmon. Was that Mr. Harmon's position, that he was never returned to any kind of post or function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know what the position of Mr. Harmon is? It looks like your objection is premature then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, No, it seems to me that Mr. Starcevic's answer could be difficult to understand, but, I mean, if not then, really, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any answer. I wish I could understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Lukic is saying there is no evidence before this court that General Mladic -- one possibility that could explain the six months is that General Mladic could have returned to active duty in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. My point is there is no evidence before this court that he did return.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. So I am happy with the state of the record as it exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if -- all right. Very well, I'm not going to complicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Starcevic, for your assistance in that particular matter. If we could turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, before you do turn, I have a problem. The previous exhibit that was displayed that talked of standby --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- Mr. Starcevic, you answered my question by saying that that person on stand by is at the disposal of. Now, this one says when he is at th disposal of, he cannot be assigned to another establishment post after an organisation unit or his establishment post has been disbanded. He cannot be assigned to other appropriate duty if it has been evaluated that he is partially fit for active military service or unfit for the duty he is discharging. Now, number 2 here contradicts number 2 in the standby rule. So in fact, here, if you are at the disposal, you can't actually -- if you are unfit or partially fit, you can't be the same person as number 2 as you explained the position -- the position of the person in paragraph 2 of the other one. So it is -- for me, it seems like these two laws contradict each other. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite sure that I understood your position. All I would like to say is that in Item 2, there are two grounds for placing at the disposal. One, is limited or partial fitness for any kind of military service; partial fitness. This implies that the person is fit to an extent. There is some extent of fitness, and they are being placed at the disposal, because, at that point in time, they cannot find a suitable post that this person would be able to be assigned to. The second grounds is that the person is unfit for the duty that they are performing, and this does not necessarily have to be a health issue. It can also be an issue of professional education, training, or qualifications, of course, the problem of competence to perform specific duties. A person can be appointed for a commander and is a bad commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we turn to the previous page of the English, please. I just want to see where this article begins. Okay. Okay. Thank you so much. Thank you. Yes. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Take this just a couple of steps further, Mr. Starcevic. Do you have any information at your disposal that after General Mladic was placed at the disposal of the VRS on 8.11.1996, he returned to duty in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about any details of the service of Mr. Mladic, and I don't know him personally. I don't have any information about these matters, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you aware that General Mladic was indicted for the crimes committed at Srebrenica and other crimes by this institution in 1996?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. I have an objection to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this question exceeds the framework or the bounds of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You raised a question a couple of minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You raised an objection, which -- wanting to say, Was the six-year term broken or not broken?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But -- that, yes. But not the fact that he put to the witness right now, whether he knows if he is accused before The Hague Tribunal now. I don't think that there is anything in my cross-examination that was put in relation to the very last question that Mr. Harmon put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a predicate to the next question I intend to ask the witness. Well, I think, in fact, Your Honours, I would like Your Honours to take notice, judicial notice of the fact that General Mladic was indicted by this institution in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not a notorious fact, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well let me put -- Your Honour, we have before this Court as an exhibit, records of the indictment and records of the correspondence that went to the Republika Srpska and that went to the FRY notifying them of the fact of those indictments. I don't have the exhibits before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you give copies of those same documents to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't that then a question of argument at the end, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I want to ask, the next question I intend to ask the witness is following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe ask the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Assuming, Mr. Starcevic, that General Mladic had been indicted by this institution for genocide and other crimes, to your knowledge, would an individual, who had such an indictment pending against them, be permitted to maintain a position in the Army of Yugoslavia and in the Army of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this, too, is outside of the bounds of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Lukic raised an objection to the proposition that I put to Mr. Starcevic. He said there's no information whatsoever before this Court that General Mladic returned to duty or could have returned to duty. What I'm trying to establish with this witness is whether there is a legal disability from him doing so, and that might assist in answering, at least partially, the objection that Mr. Lukic raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, I guess Mr. Lukic' objection - and he can speak for himself - is based on the fact that in your question, you link up this whole question of indictments, which he says he never asked about. You know, I think if you can put your question in such a way that you eliminate indictments, and you talk about Mr. Mladic's return to duty in the six-year period, without referring to indictments, you probably are not going to pick up an objection. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, would there be -- what limitations would there be for General Mladic to return to active duty in either the VRS or in the VJ? What would be those limitations? We've talked about fitness, one of them.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the second reason could be unfitness, and that could be practical, professional, or any other unfitness to perform duties assigned. If there is a legal decision in force against that particular person, then he would not be able to return to duty, and that person would be removed from duty, they would not be placed at the disposal. So I think that, in that case, you would not be considering the grounds or the option of placing at the disposal at all, but you would be considering the option of having that particular person removed from duty, which is a different form of grounds for not returning or being removed from service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you say, just to clarify your answer, when you say "If there is a legal decision in force against a particular person," what type of legal decision are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be precise, I said if there is an legal indictment or a charging document, and there is a document -- a differences in our legal system between these two documents, then such a person would be removed from duties until that case is resolved finally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you still want to stay in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At this -- yes, because I am now going to finish with this line of questioning, Your Honour. I'm going to question Mr. Starcevic about another exhibit that was shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Half past.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Half past. Thank you. Could we have D125, MFI, under seal, on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We looked at this document a minute ago, Mr. Starcevic. This is a document that is from General Perisic and it says to -- and the first paragraph is directed to the Main Staff of the SVK. And it says: "Please influence the political leadership of the Republic of Serbian Krajina." Let me ask you, Mr. Starcevic, have you ever seen such a similar document requesting that a unit influence the political leadership of another country?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember, but I don't think that I've ever seen such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, such -- let's look at this document on its face. Could General Perisic have ordered the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of the Krajina to influence the political leadership of a different country? Could he have said this differently through an order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have order, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that there were any grounds for him to send an order and that he couldn't have issued a command or ordered the Main Staff of another army, the army of another state.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. When you say -- just to finalise this, you don't think there is any grounds for him to send an order, an order to influence another state? Is that what -- that's the type of order I'm asking you about. Could he have given an order to a subordinate unit to influence political leadership of another state?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think -- I think that this question exceeds the bounds of my cross-examination. I did not ask Mr. Starcevic about the content of the document. I also think that with this document and this question -- in this question, Mr. Starcevic is being asked to enter into the area of constitutional relationships, and I think that he is less competent as an expert on the political leadership and those matters, and that was not the topic of my cross-examination, and this is the gist of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can you give us a reference to where you asked that question, because I'm having a different recollection of your cross-examination on this document from what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, Your Honour. I would like it find it. Pages 7 and 8. My question was -- page 6, line 20, this is what my assistants are telling me. I'm asking about the form of the document I think that the question that Mr. Harmon is putting now does not arise from the questions that I put to the witness, so I -- I stand by my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph -- page 7, sir, line 1 that's what I wanted to put the next question about. Based on these contents, and the way Mr. Perisic is addressing Mr. Mrksic, we request -- see that from the words kindly and -- well, that's how it was interpreted but it says, please, and so on, and so forth influence, can it be seen interest of this kind of address there was any kind of hierarchical relationship between Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Perisic in those hierarchical relationship command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between the two armies, that was my question. But I think that Mr. Harmon is now going for the relationship and the influence on a different political leadership, on another political leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think, then, that the objection is semantic. I'll overruled it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Starcevic. Mr. Starcevic, can you -- you remember my question? If not, I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Could -- could General Perisic --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I do apologise, Mr. Harmon, but I think this may become an issue at a later point in time. And, unfortunately, Judge Moloto's ruling did not get on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I did say clearly the objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand it's not there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I now appreciate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that you thought it was a semantic issue and you had overruled it, and I just -- I have a feeling this may become an issue at a later point in time, and I do apologise to all the parties for interrupting because this is not my witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. The objection is overruled, if the record can show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to get you home, Mr. Starcevic, and we're not making much progress in that direction. So let me ask this question.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could General Perisic have given a order to a subordinate unit to influence the political leadership of another state?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to understand a command to one's own subordinate unit, to influence the political leadership of another state. I simply cannot understand that relationship. General Perisic had the right to issue any kind of order or command to his units, to influence -- or to a unit of his to influence in -- to influence any kind of organ of a country with which they were in conflict. If there is no conflict that any kind of order of that kind is illegitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. I think I've finished with that line of questioning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we go into open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This might be an appropriate time for a break, Your Honour. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, I need your assistance to make a minor correction in your earlier testimony, since you are here, and you're the only one who can do that. I would like to direct your attention --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to direct the Court's attention to page 5545 of the transcript, line 21. Counsel, that's the particular line I referenced earlier during the break. Could I have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line 5541?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sorry, it's page 5545, line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 5541, line 21. I'll do it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will read the text of this, Your Honours, and I'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, if I could have --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all, if I can have 197, Prosecution Exhibit 197, on the monitor; and, specifically, I'd like to focus on Article 181, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Starcevic, let me explain just what the topic of discussion was. The topic of discussion that -- you gave the following answer. We were talking about who had the authority, which persons were authorised to bring persons before -- who had committed disciplinary offences before a military disciplinary court and in your answer, starts on page 5545 at line 18, you said: "However, an officer who orders that a disciplinary investigation be launched is not responsible or is not authorised to formally place the perpetrator under the jurisdiction of a disciplinary court. Those powers rest with the officers who are defined in Article 182."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And we scroll to 182.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you see 182, Mr. Starcevic? Did you -- you're nodding your head. Do you see the error that is in that --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is the proper article that you should have referred to under the circumstances -- under the -- in your answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That corrects the mistake, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could have -- actually I want to focus on the special purpose industry. You testified yesterday about the special purpose industry. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And then you were shown Defence Exhibit 114, which was the decree on the adoption of the Law on Property for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and that Article 39, in that law, defined what movable items for special purposes included, that included weapons military, equipment to be used by the Ministry of Defence and the Yugoslav Army; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I cannot see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we have Defence Exhibit 114 on the monitor, please, and can we focus on Article 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is the article that Mr. Lukic directed your attention to and defines in the first sentence what movable items were and under whose authority this is -- this material is -- falls under. The jurisdiction under whose -- let me start again. Who can distribute this material, who can manage and maintain this material; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. This article, in its entirety, yes. But you were referring only to paragraph 2, where it specifies these assets, and paragraph 2 speaks about who is entitled to dispose of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who is entitled to dispose of it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under this law, it is the federal minister for defence, and the federal minister for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you that clarifies it. Now, let me ask you, within this framework of what we're talking about, do the special purposes, the military industry production plants fall within this set of articles we have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Basically those were the facilities used by the MOD. But they are not governed by this article, because this article refers only to movable assets, whereas plants and other facilities are immovable assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But they're under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, was the special production plant, Krusik, one of those special production facilities that fell under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think yes. I cannot be quite positive here, because basically all these companies were of a mixed nature. In other words, the companies that were involved both in civilian production and partly with the protection of military equipment and weapons. But I think that this particular part that was involved in the production of military equipment and weapons, the federal Ministry of Defence had jurisdiction, or, to be more precise, a specific directorate within the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we go into private session.

utterances.text: Just before we do so, how was this article implemented, sir, being controlled by two ministries, either or both of them? utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that the law indicates that this is about the equipment being used, according to paragraph 1 of this article, by the MOD for the purposes of defence, and, on the other hand, the federal ministry of internal affairs for security purposes. utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to underline that I'm not completely competent to discuss this topic. But, as I understand it, one should make a distinction between disposing of and procurement of items that are intended for defence of a country, and, on the other hand, the sale of weapons and military equipment to someone outside that particular country. If I remember correctly, in order for the special purpose industry to sell its products that are of interest for defence, it required approval from certain organs in the state. Judging by this letter, it seemed that the approval of the General Staff was also required, but I'm not sure about that. I only understand this to mean that the sales of equipment or military equipment and weapons to anyone was subject to certain international obligations undertaken by the country. And that was precisely the reason why the special purpose industry could not, without appropriate approval, sell these items on the free markets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we go into public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute. If you say, sir, that there are certain international obligations, how does the Chief of Staff of the General Staff get involved in political, international obligations? utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said that I am not very comfortable in this particular area. This is not my expertise. But I can only offer my understanding of this issue. I suppose that this kind of approvals from higher instances in -- in reaching the final decision is up to one single organ. This is how I understand this, but I said I have this reservation regarding my limited knowledge about this specific area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me put the question slightly differently: From your knowledge of the Law on Defence, and the Army of the former Yugoslavia, is there any provision in there that would require the Chief of Staff of the General Staff to give approval for exportation of military equipment from the former Yugoslavia to an outside country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are no such provisions in the laws that you have cited. This is governed and regulated by another law relating to the production of military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic I want to direct your attention to some questions and answers that you gave yesterday. I'm directing counsel's attention to the answers that are in -- and questions found at pages 6876 to 6879 of the transcript. You were asked by my colleague Mr. Lukic where and I quote: "There was a severe and fierce civil war raging in 1992 all the way through the year in which the Dayton Accords were signed." And you said: "Yes, unfortunately, that was the case." And then Mr. Lukic asked: "Would you agree with me that that represented a permanent danger of the war spilling over into the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?" Your answer was: "I may draw some conclusions on that, but I can agree with you that posed a danger in relation -- in two relations between Yugoslavia and the war-torn zones. And if I may add this, I think that up until the official recognition of the new states, Croatia, Slovenia, and later, Bosnia and Herzegovina, that was, in essence, a civil war in the former Yugoslavia." Now, in your answer, you appeared to be making a distinction, Mr. Starcevic, a distinction up until the official recognition of the new states and it being a civil war. What distinction were you trying to make in respect of this answer, if any?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it will take a long time for me to give you a complete explanation, but I will try and do my best to put aside that I'm a professor and give you the shortest possible answer. As someone who is engaged and involved in international law, I can say that everything that started at the time in the former Yugoslavia had the nature of a civil war, and all the conflicts initially were of that nature, until certain point in time. The decisive moment occurred when certain states or republics were internationally recognised. But in most cases, that also coincided with the cessation of hostilities. Let me remind you, for example, that the conflict in Slovenia had already stopped. That, at the time when Croatia was recognised as an independent and separate state, also the conflict ceased, that the war lasted in Bosnia-Herzegovina; but that, pursuant to the decisions of the authorities in charge, the remaining part of what used to be the SFRY actually withdrew from those areas. Unfortunately, this did not bring an end to the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because the civil war went on there, but without the involvement of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Therefore, it was a civil war among warring parties in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And, finally, the event that we mentioned, just occasionally and superficially, but we mentioned it several times, and I think was the case of the infamous Operations Flash and Storm also had elements of a civil war between the official armed forces of Croatia and the forces of the Army of the Serbian Republic of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying Croatia had not been recognised by the time of Operation Storm as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what I'm saying. I'm only saying that the conflict was ragging in the territory of that state and that it was an internal conflict between two forces within one state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Focussing on Bosnia just briefly, if, in fact, forces from an outside country were involved in that conflict, would the characterization of the conflict be different?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not easy to give a simple answer to this question, because there had been precedent before that conflict. Let me just remind you of the case of Nicaragua without going into broadcast discussions about this particular case. It is necessary for the intensity on interference and involvement for it to justify the conflict to be characterized and considered as international one. Speaking about Bosnia-Herzegovina, it is difficult to say that this level of intensity had been achieved, particularly after the well-known judgement rendered by the International Court of Justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a yes or no, would you say the current war in Afghanistan is international or civil, with the involvement of the US in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The war in Afghanistan has both types of features. That is what we experts in international law are trying to define, what internationalised conflicts are. That is to say, they initially start as internal conflicts, but with the involvement of third parties, they become internationalised. There is it no doubt that the level of involvement or the degree of involvement into what, initially, was a civil war in Afghanistan is really close to the point when it can be considered as an international one. However, one has to bear in mind another fact and that is the involvement of the UN in keeping with the UN charter, and that has a tremendous effect on the ultimate formulation and definition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harmon.

Can you assist me, why would a VRS document putting General Milosevic on disposal in the VRS rely on an Article in the VJ law and not on the Law of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
