utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, he would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The next paragraph deals with what you two gentlemen are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The next paragraph, indeed, Your Honour, it does. It's part of the judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No objection [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection that is being considered in that next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me turn to some different documents, if I can. You were shown some documents that related to General Mladic's special compensation for service in special circumstances. The first document you were shown was P741, and if we can have that on the monitor please. This document you're familiar with, you have seen now at least twice in these proceedings, Mr. Starcevic. This is the decision of General Perisic on determining the task and territory where services are performed under special circumstances. Let me just -- just to reorient you a little bit. If we could go down to the -- up -- scroll up a little bit on the B/C/S version, yes, and we could focus on the last paragraph in English. This -- you're familiar with this document, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You will see in terms of defining where service is performed under difficult circumstances, it sets forth five sub-points, the fifth sub-point being the territory where members of the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres are in service. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now let me show you some decisions that we also looked at -- you looked at with Mr. Lukic. The first part --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecution Exhibit 1810 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I want it clarify a point with this document and one of your answers you gave to Mr. Lukic. It's found at page 6957, lines 16 to 21. So this document that's in front of us -- before I turn to the testimony that you gave, before I turn to the testimony, this document is the decision of the Military Post 3001, awarding General Mladic special compensation. And this really has -- the decision reflects or concentrates on three different bases or three different compensations. You will see in subpart A the amount of 20 per cent; subpart B, there is an reference to compensation -- increases compensation, there is a reference to Article 24 in the decision of the Military Post 3001, and it gives a date and refreshes number; and in -- thirdly, it gives an amount of four per cent basic increase in salary. Now my first question to you is: In the preamble, it sets forth, does it not, on what basis this decision is founded? Is that -- what is that basis on which this decision is founded, according to the preamble?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Article 156 of the Law on the Yugoslav Army and the decision of the Chief of Staff which governs the methodology of exercising the rights --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if you could go to the second page, please, of this document, you will see that under subpart B of this, when it refers to -- the second part which is the second paragraph in English. I hope it appears in your document; it may not, actually. Does it -- do you see in your text, Mr. Starcevic, the increase of compensation stipulated under B, and I think we've found it now. Now, you were asked the following question by Mr. Lukic, and this is where I need the clarification. You were asked the question: "And under B, it says the basis for issuing this decision by Military Post 3001 is a decision of the commander of Military Post 3001; am I right? " And your answer was, "Yes." Let me ask you this question: Mr. Starcevic, is that what this says or does this subpart B say that the increase in compensation, under B, in the disposition of this decision has been recognised as he is serving with the unit covered by the decision of the commander, and it goes on. Is the decision -- do you understand my question, Mr. Starcevic? There is an slightly different meaning between the two. I'm just seeking out what is the correct meaning of this. Was the decision to award compensation under B based on the decision; or was it because he was serving in a unit that is covered by the decision?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I find it hard to understand your question. In the statement of reasons that you referred to, it says that this increase, stipulated under sub-item B, has been granted due to the fact that he was carrying out his duties in the unit that is covered by the decision of the commander of the VP 3001. Therefore, this is only an explanation of this increase that was granted under subparagraph B.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's the clarification I was seeking. Now, if we could go to the third document that was shown in this case to you; I just want to identify which unit that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could go to P2046, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is the decision, Mr. Starcevic, that was referred to in the previous document, and which -- in which unit was General Mladic serving at the time he received this special compensation? If you refer to -- under the words "decision," paragraph 1, it would give you the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military Post 7572, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that clarification, Mr. Starcevic. If we can turn to a different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I can have -- let me just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we look at two documents you looked at, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: P363 is the first document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, you were asked some questions about particular words that appeared in this particular document, those words being found in the second paragraph under certificate. And the words you were asked about was: He was wounded carrying out combat activities securing the SRJ state border. Now, Mr. Starcevic, one of the questions that you were asked by Mr. Lukic was --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, before we do that, could we also take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 557.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to bounce around like this, Your Honour. I'm told this document is under seal. So we have to go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We will take a break and come back at a quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're almost there, Mr. Starcevic. Let me ask you, in your earlier testimony, Mr. Starcevic, you indicated that there were three situations under Yugoslav Army law where persons in the VJ could be sent abroad. One was -- they could be sent to diplomatic or consular offices; second, they could be sent to duties relating to international agreement, peacekeeping, for example; and the third was, they could be sent for education. My question, Mr. Starcevic, is when VJ soldiers are sent abroad to participate in peacekeeping operations, who has the disciplinary authority, the sending state or the receiving organisation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Mr. Harmon has put to the witness now is related to the examination-in-chief and not to cross-examination. I would appreciate a reference to my cross-examination, otherwise, I have an objection to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see a smile on your face, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, at the beginning of your testimony, on page 14, lines 21, 22, on the 8th June, the Prosecution has presented you in Exhibit 1827 a so-called warning. You said at page 15, lines 13 to 17, in relation to this document: "It does not have the legal significance of a warning. It is a colloquial act or document, advice, proposal, or recommendation." Later on, you said, in response to Judge Moloto's question, at page 18, line 1 to 6: "Warning is, in a way, a question of good service or an advice. Perhaps there could be some influence on the quality of the relationship between the person who is issuing the warning and/or the side that is issuing the warning, and the side that does not adhere to the warning." My question, Mr. Starcevic, is the following: How this colloquial act or advice or recommendation fits into the functions given by Article 175 of the Yugoslav Army to the commander in chief when speaks this article of regulation, order, instructions, and other documents as part of the responsibilities or authority of the chief of General Staff of the army? Is that clear, my question, to you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is clear. But I'm afraid that, when you quoted the first answer, either I was not accurate or there may have, perhaps, been some misunderstanding in terms of interpretation, I didn't mean to say, as I have been quoted, that it does not have a legal significance of a warning. What I simply wanted to say was that a warning does not have a legal significance or a legal character or nature. That was the essence of what I wanted to say. Therefore, a warning is not a document envisaged by the law, nor does it require a proper legal procedure to be issued. There is no such category as a warning among the powers vested in the chief of General Staff or any other officer that is authorised to command, and precisely for that reason, this is not a legal document but, rather, a colloquial document issued by someone who is giving a warning to another person is probably wishing to help in solving a problem, or to draw this person's attention to potential adverse consequences in the event of this warning not being heeded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: So, Mr. Starcevic, your conclusion is, if I understood well your answer, that this act does not enter into the enumeration or comprehensiveness of Article 175. Is that correct or ...

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: My second question: You have said yesterday something that, perhaps, I would like you to elaborate in relation to this document. You said at page 86, line 2 to 6: "The crux of the problem is legal status in factual situations," referring yourself to the understanding of many -- many orders or commands, et cetera, that should be, if I understood you, not only from a formal viewpoint from the letter of the law but from the factual structural situation. Could you elaborate? I don't want to confuse, you but it interested me very much your characterization, you know? Or a principle of interpretation, which is to say, the crux of the matter is legal status in factual situations. Could you apply this construction, I will call it your theoretical construction, Mr. Starcevic, to the problem inside?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should probably be made aware to what question I gave that answer. What was the question, I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, you were clarifying certain situations of regulations and these positions that needed some articulation between what the norm [phoen] said and what the particular situations of the case was. My question, in this regard, has to do with the factual effects of a warning. Could you, in your experience, elaborate what could be the factual effect of a warning if you, in the circumstances that you knew, beyond the lack of legal validity, you already hint when -- into the problem when you said influence, you know, you said here exactly: "Perhaps there could be some influence on the quality of the relationship between the person who is issuing the warning and -- or the side that has issued the warning and the side that does not adhere to the warning." Page 18, lines 1 to 6.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that now I understand your point. So, even though a warning does not have any legal foundation or significance - in other words, the one who issues it, cannot invoke any authority under which he is entitled to give this warning, because this kind of authority simply does not exist. Therefore, the consequence of issuing such an order --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, such a warning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- does not constitute a legal obligation to the receiving side. However, in a factual situation, this may lead, even to a deterioration of the relationship between the issuing party and the receiving party of the warning and if the receiving party ignores this warning. I'm trying to think of an example to explain this in a more simple and easier way. If, for instance, within the framework of cooperation between police forces between two countries, these relationships are not legally regulated, but, nevertheless, the police in one country acquires intelligence that, for example, in this other state a terrorist group is being active and making preparations for committing a terrorist act. In the country which is sending the warning, the only possibility that they have at their disposal is just to send a warning to the police of another country of what is in the offing. If the police does not take this warning seriously, at least to such an extent to launch an investigation and eventually this terrorist act does happen, one can imagine that this will affect the quality of relationships between the two parties. So that is what I meant when I say that in a factual situation, a warning may result in a deterioration of relationships, and, quite vice versa, if a warning is heeded and adhered to, can improve these relations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Another example of the factual situation, would it also be that if the warning is not heeded, the consequences against which the person is being warned might eventuate, in which case, there may be tragedy; or if they are heeded, that tragedy may be avoided. That would be --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions arising?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions arising, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Starcevic, thank you so much. You have come here twice in this case. We thank you so much for the time you have given to the trial. We've come now to the end of your testimony. You are excused. You may stand down. Please travel back home well. I hope you have some rest before you start your duties back home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That concludes our evidence for this week. We have no additional witnesses for today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. In that event, then, the case stands adjourned to Monday, the 15th of June, at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, Courtroom I. Court adjourned.
